messages.content: Did you see that girl in the red tam? the one with the high color who had the two police dogs down to bid her good-by.
She's pretty.
No, sir. I don't want to caddy any more. I'm too old.
You're not more than fourteen. Why the devil did you decide just this morning that you wanted to quit? You promised that next week you'd go over to the State tournament with me.
I don't know what we're supposed to do now.
Oh, that's all right. I'll fix it up.
Boy, do you know where the golf teacher is?
He's giving a lesson.
Well, do you know where the caddy-master is?
He isn't here yet this morning.
Oh.
We'd like to get a caddy. Mrs. Mortimer Jones sent us out to play golf, and we don't know how without we get a caddy.
There aren't any caddies here except me, and I got to stay here in charge until the caddy-master gets here.
Oh.
Miss Jones is to have a little caddy, and this one says he can't go.
Mr. McKenna said I was to wait here till you came.
Well, he's here now.
Well? What you standing there like a dummy for? Go pick up the young lady's clubs.
I don't think I'll go out to-day.
You don't----
Do you mind if we go through?
You hit me in the stomach!
That Judy Jones! All she needs is to be turned up and spanked for six months and then to be married off to an old-fashioned cavalry captain.
My God, she's good-looking!
She'd play pretty good golf if she'd try.
She has no form.
She has a nice figure.
Better thank the Lord she doesn't drive a swifter ball.
Do you mind if I weep a little?
I'm afraid I'm boring you.
I'm nobody. My career is largely a matter of futures.
Are you poor?
Dexter. Irene's gone up-stairs with a splitting headache. She wanted to go with you but I made her go to bed.
Nothing serious, I----
When did you get back?
Come here and I'll tell you about it.
Have you a car here? If you haven't, I have.
I have a coupe.
Have you missed me?
Everybody missed you.
What a remark!
You're handsomer than you used to be. Dexter, you have the most rememberable eyes.
Of course you could never love anybody but me. I like the way you love me. Oh, Dexter, have you forgotten last year?
No, I haven't forgotten.
I wish we could be like that again.
I don't think we can.
Judy Simms. Judy Jones she was once.
Yes, I knew her.
Awfully nice girl. I'm sort of sorry for her.
Why?
Oh, Lud Simms has gone to pieces in a way. I don't mean he ill-uses her, but he drinks and runs around-----
Doesn't she run around?
No. Stays at home with her kids.
Oh.
She's a little too old for him.
Too old! Why, man, she's only twenty-seven.
I guess you're busy. I didn't realize----
No, I'm not busy. I'm not busy at all. Not busy at all. Did you say she was--twenty-seven? No, I said she was twenty-seven.
Yes, you did.
Go on, then. Go on.
What do you mean?
About Judy Jones.
Isn't she--a pretty girl, any more?
Oh, she's all right.
Bow-wow? There isn't any bow-wow.
Bow-wow. I want a bow-wow.
That isn't a bow-wow, dearest, that's a teddy-bear.
Bear?
Did he bump his head?
No-o-o-o. He bumped something else, didn't you, Billy? He bumped something else.
Please go home! The child's badly hurt, and if you haven't the decency to be quiet, you'd better go home.
Very well. I've never seen any one make such a mountain out of----
Why, Mrs. Andros, can't you see the child's hurt? You really ought to control yourself.
Control m-myself! You better ask her to c-control herself. I've never heard anybody so c-common in my life.
She's insulting me! Did you hear what she said, Joe? I wish you'd put her out. If she won't go, just take her by the shoulders and put her out!
Don't you dare touch me! I'm going just as quick as I can find my c-coat!
John!
What's the matter? Why, what's the matter?
They're--they're putting me out! He'd just started to take me by the shoulders and put me out. I want my coat!
That's not true. Nobody's going to put you out. Nobody's going to put her out. She's----
What do you mean 'put her out'? What's all this talk, anyhow?
Oh, let's go! I want to go. They're so common, John!
Look here! You've said that about enough. You're acting sort of crazy.
They called Ede a brat!
What's the idea of this? Do you insult your guests in your own house?
It seems to me it's your wife that's done the insulting! In fact, your baby there started all the trouble.
Don't talk to him, John. Find my coat!
You must be in a bad way, if you have to take out your temper on a helpless little baby.
I never heard anything so damn twisted in my life. If that wife of yours would shut her mouth for a minute----
Wait a minute! You're not talking to a woman and child now----
I'll be damned if I'm going on with this thing any more.
I'm not going on any more either. I've had enough of this thing.
Want to come in and wash up?
No, thanks. I ought to be going home--my wife'll be worried.
No harm done.
No--you?
No, no harm done.
Well. I guess I'll say good night.
But you must have been crazy. I thought you were going to fix it all up there and shake hands. That's why I went away.
Did you want us to fix it up?
I don't understand yet how it all happened.
Neither do I. I guess these baby parties are pretty rough affairs.
Well, one thing-- I'm certainly glad we have beefsteak in the house for to-morrow's dinner.
Why?
Is she asleep?
Sound asleep. But you can go in and peek at her--just to say good night.
She's asleep.
Naturally, after such an afternoon.
Why, what incomparable nerve! Just tell them we're not home. I wouldn't go down for anything in the world.
You most certainly will.
What?
You'll go down right now, and, what's more, whatever that other woman does, you'll apologize for what you said this afternoon. After that you don't ever have to see her again.
Why--John, I can't.
You've got to. And just remember that she probably hated to come over here just twice as much as you hate to go down-stairs.
Father Schwartz--I've committed a terrible sin.
A sin against purity?
Have you killed somebody?
No--but I'm afraid--
How, my child?

Old lady Swenson. She got our baseball that we knocked in her window, and she wouldn't give it back, so we yelled 'Twenty-three, Skidoo,' at her all afternoon. Then about five o'clock she had a fit, and they had to have the doctor.
Go on, my child.
Of--of not believing I was the son of my parents.
What?
Of not believing that I was the son of my parents.
Why not?
Oh, just pride.
You mean you thought you were too good to be the son of your parents?
Yes, Father.
Go on.
Of being disobedient and calling my mother names. Of slandering people behind my back. Of smoking----
Of dirty words and immodest thoughts and desires.
How often?
I don't know.
Once a week? Twice a week?
Twice a week.
Did you yield to these desires?
No, Father.
Were you alone when you had them?
No, Father. I was with two boys and a girl.

Don't you know, my child, that you should avoid the occasions of sin as well as the sin itself? Evil companionship leads to evil desires and evil desires to evil actions. Where were you when this happened?
In a barn in back of----
I don't want to hear any names.
Well, it was up in the loft of this barn and this girl and--a fella, they were saying things--saying immodest things, and I stayed.
You should have gone--you should have told the girl to go.
Have you anything else to tell me?
I don't think so, Father.
What are you doing?
I got awful thirsty, so I thought I'd just come down and get----
I forgot all about it.
Have you drunk any water?
What's the matter with you, anyways?
Nothing.
Did you go to confession yesterday?
Yes.
Then why were you going to drink water?
I don't know--I forgot.
Maybe you care more about being a little bit thirsty than you do about your religion.
I forgot.
That's no answer.
Well, I did.
I can remember it all right.
First you begin to neglect your religion, the next thing you'll begin to lie and steal, and the next thing is the reform school!
I've decided you'd better go to confession again. Go in and tell Father Schwartz what you did and ask God's pardon.
You lost your temper, too!
All right, I'll go.
Are you going to do what I say?
I accuse myself of missing my morning prayers.
Is that all?

I said-- Do you hear the hammer and the clock ticking and the bees? Well, that's no good. The thing is to have a lot of people in the centre of the world, wherever that happens to be. Then things go glimmering.
Yes, Father.
What are you going to be when you grow up?
Well, I was going to be a baseball-player for a while, but I don't think that's a very good ambition, so I think I'll be an actor or a Navy officer.
This man is crazy, and I'm scared of him. He wants me to help him out some way, and I don't want to.
You look as if things went glimmering. Did you ever go to a party?
I've been to a lot of parties.
Of course. I knew you'd agree with me. But my theory is that when a whole lot of people get together in the best places things go glimmering all the time.
Look here-- Did you ever see an amusement park?
No, Father.
Rags. Rags----
John M. Chestnut?
I've got a lot of junk to declare.
So have I, and the first thing I want to declare is that I've loved you, Rags, every minute since you've been away.
Please! There were some young Americans on the boat. The subject has become a bore.
My God! do you mean to say that you class my love with what was said to you on a boat?
John if you raise your voice again I'll arrange it so you'll have plenty of chance to cool off. I'm going to the Ritz. Come and see me there this afternoon.
But, Rags! Listen to me. Five years ago----
I wrote you that I didn't intend to stay more than a week anyhow.
But, Rags----
Why should I? There isn't an amusing man in New York.
But listen, Rags, won't you give me a chance? Won't you stay for, say, ten days and get to know me a little?
Know you! I want a man who's capable of a gallant gesture.
Do you mean you want me to express myself entirely in pantomime?
I mean you haven't any imagination. No Americans have any imagination. Paris is the only large city where a civilized woman can breathe.
Don't you care for me at all any more?
I'd love to be in love. Last spring in Sorrento I almost eloped with an Indian rajah, but he was half a shade too dark, and I took an intense dislike to one of his other wives.
Don't talk that rubbish!
Well, I didn't marry him. But in one way he had a lot to offer. He was the third richest subject of the British Empire. That's another thing--are you rich?
Not as rich as you.
There you are. What have you to offer me?
Love.
Don't throw yourself out.
All right.
Well, just for a rest you come out with me to-night.
Where to? Do you think I still thrill at a night-club and a bottle of sugary mousseaux? I prefer my own gaudy dreams.
I'll take you to the most highly-strung place in the city.
What'll happen? You've got to tell me what'll happen.
For the last time--will you come along with me to-night and see what you will see?
See what? See who? Is there anything in this country worth seeing?
Well, for one thing you'll see the Prince of Wales.
What? Is he back in New York?
He will be to-night. Would you care to see him?
Would I? I've never seen him. I've missed him everywhere. I'd give a year of my life to see him for an hour.
What makes it so warm?
It's some new invention that keeps the warm air from rising. I don't know the principle of the thing, but I know that they can keep it open like this even in the middle of winter--
Who's that?
That's Roderigo Minerlino, the movie and face-cream star. Perhaps he'll dance after a while.
He's gone!
Don't worry--he'll be back. He's got to be awfully careful, you see, so he's probably waiting outside with one of his aides until it gets dark again.
Why has he got to be careful?
Because he's not supposed to be in New York. He's even under one of his second-string names.
That is between ourselves, you understand.
Of course.
Well, what did he say?
He was very quiet.
He just looked at me while it was dark. And he said a few conventional things. He was like his pictures, only he looks very bored and tired. He didn't even ask my name.
Is he leaving New York to-night?
In half an hour. He and his aides have a car outside, and they expect to be over the border before dawn.
Did you find him--fascinating?
That's what everybody says. Do they expect you back there?
I don't know.
Monte! What is it? What's the matter?
They've picked up the trail! I've got to speak to you alone.
Are you sick?
Rags. I'm all through.
What do you mean?
I'm all through, I tell you. There's been a warrant out for me for over an hour.
What is it?
Murder?
Oh, God! why don't you do something?
If I arrange it, will you go to Canada to-night?
How?
I'll arrange it--if you'll pull yourself together a little. This is Rags talking to you, don't you understand, John? I want you to sit here and not move until I come back!
His lordship's car is full.
It's terribly urgent.
Is that one of your revenue fellas out there?
No. There's going to be trouble. Can't we get out this entrance?
Here! Take a look at that funny bunch across over there. Hands up, you men!
My God! we've got to get out of here! This won't do, Ted. You can't be seen here. I'll stall them off while you get down to the car.
Hands up, there! And when I say hands up I mean it! Which one of you's Chestnut?
You're mad! We're British subjects. We're not involved in this affair in any way!
What was it? Am I dreaming?
Of course not! You're wide awake. I made it up, Rags, don't you see? I made up the whole thing for you. I had it invented! The only thing real about it was my name!
Are you sure you're real? Are you absolutely sure?
You only wrote me a week before you came, or I could have arranged a revolution.
The next stop is the City Hall. Then, if you like, we'll run over to Paris.
John, who was the Prince of Wales?
Patronize this place, lady. Best bazaar in the city!
What have you got for sale?
Well, m'selle, to-day we have some perfectly bee-oo-tiful love.
Wrap it up, Mr. Merchant. It looks like a bargain to me.
Shall I tell you something outrageous?
Try.
Is that you, dear?
Yes, dear.
Good evening, Mrs. Hemple. I hope I'm not interfering with any arrangement of yours.
Oh, no. I'm delighted that you're coming to dinner. We're quite alone.
Has he been good?
Very good. We went for a long walk over by Central Park.
Well, aren't you a smart boy!
And he put his foot into the fountain, so we had to come home in a taxi right away and change his little shoe and stocking.
Such a nice house, Mrs. Hemple, and let me congratulate you on your fine little boy.
Thanks. Coming from a doctor, that's a nice compliment. Do you specialize in children?
I'm not a specialist at all. I'm about the last of my kind--a general practitioner.
The last in New York, anyhow.
A talk with me?
Doctor Moon's an old friend of mine, and I think he can tell you a few things, Luella, that you ought to know.
Don't be afraid, Mrs. Hemple. This was forced upon me. I do not act as a free agent----
I'm not afraid of you.
Didn't you see him rubbing his face at dinner? Are you blind? He's become so irritating to me that I think I'll go mad.
I see.
Yes?
Can I speak to--? Mr. Hemple, he's sick! He came into the kitchen a while ago and began throwing all the food out of the ice-box, and now he's in his room, crying and singing----
Luella! Luella! Where are you?
I'm right here, Charles, beside you.
I'm only going for a minute. It's Doctor Moon, your friend, Charles. He came to-day to see how you were, don't you remember? And he wants to talk to me before he goes.
You'll come back?
Mrs. Hemple.
You seem well.
I am well, thank you.
I congratulate you on the way you've taken hold of things.
But I haven't taken hold of things at all. I do what I have to----
That's just it.
Would you mind telling me how you found out the nurse didn't know her business?
You find out various unpleasant things when you're forced to stay around the house.
What do you mean? You've done nothing for me--nothing at all!
Nothing much--yet. It takes time, Mrs. Hemple.
Mrs. Danski is my name.
What's the matter?
I'm afraid I won't be able to accommodate you. You see, I'm only a plain cook, and I'm not used to preparing invalid's food.
But I've counted on you.
I got my own children to think of, just like you.
I've never heard of anything so selfish in my life! To leave me at a time like this! You're an old fool!
If you'd pay me for my time, I'd go.
I won't pay you a cent unless you'll stay!
You will so pay me!
You go out that door!
Can you send me some one right away? My husband is sick and the baby's sick----
I'm sorry, Mrs. Hemple; there's no one in the office now. It's after four o'clock.
How's baby?
Ninety-nine one. I just took it.
Is that much?
It's just three-fifths of a degree. That isn't so much for the afternoon. They often run up a little with a cold.
Do you know how to cook?
Why--I'm not a good cook.
Well, can you do the baby's food to-night? That old fool has left, and I can't get anyone, and I don't know what to do.
Oh, yes, I can do the baby's food.
Yes, this is Mrs. Hemple speaking.
Why, the woman we sent to you has returned here with the claim that you refused to pay her for her time.

We have to see that our people are paid, otherwise we wouldn't be helping them at all, would we? I'm sorry, Mrs. Hemple, but we won't be able to furnish you with any one else until this little matter is arranged.
Oh, I'll pay, I'll pay!
Of course we like to keep on good terms with our clients----
Yes--yes!
So if you'll send her money around to-morrow? It's seventy-five cents an hour.
But how about to-night? I've got to have some one to-night.
Why--it's pretty late now. I was just going home myself.
But I'm Mrs. Charles Hemple! Don't you understand? I'm perfectly good for what I say I'll do. I'm the wife of Charles Hemple, of 14 Broadway----
Fainted, that's all. Yep, she fainted, that's all.
Everybody's sick! Everybody's sick but me, doctor.
You go away.
Your husband needs you.
I don't think you understand, Mrs. Hemple. He's been calling for you. You haven't any one now except him.
I hate you.
My baby isn't dead! You lie! You always lie!
All right. My baby is gone. What shall I do now?
Your husband is much better. All he needs is rest and kindness. But you must go to him and tell him what's happened.
I suppose you think you made him better.
The baby is dead?
Yes.
The doctor said he could be taken out for a drive to-day while there was still sunshine. He needs a little change.
Yes.
I thought you'd gone. I told you to go away.
I'm going soon, but I don't want you to make an old mistake.
I'm not making a mistake--I'm leaving my mistakes behind.
You're trying to leave yourself behind, but you can't. The more you try to run away from yourself, the more you'll have yourself with you.
But I've got to go away. Out of this house of death and failure!
You haven't failed yet. You've only begun.
Let me pass.
No.
Go back into that room and tell the nurse you'll take your husband for a drive.
I can't.
Do you mean for good?
For good.
But I want the light and glitter. That's all there is in life. There can't be anything wrong in wanting to have things warm.
Things will still be warm.
How?
Things will warm themselves from you.
I see new lines in my face here, and a few shadows at the sides that might be--that are little wrinkles.
Do you care?
Do you realize that Chuck is gone? That you'll never see him any more?
Yes. But that all seems so vague and far away.
Vague and far away. And are you afraid of me now?
Not any longer, now that you're going away.
Won't you sit down a moment longer?
There isn't time. But remember that whatever suffering comes to you, I can always help you--if it is something that can be helped. I promise nothing.
What have you done to me? Why have I no sorrow left for Chuck--for anything at all? Tell me; I almost see, yet I can't see. Before you go--tell me who you are!
Who am I?--
Ede and her husband are coming to dinner. I've got theatre tickets, but if you're tired, I don't care whether we go or not.
I'd like to go.
You wouldn't.
I really would.
He just dropped in for a minute. How's everything at home?
All right. What did he want?
Oh, he just wanted to see me about something.
What?
Oh, just something. Business.
Why were his eyes red?
Were they?
You might as well tell me, because I'm going to stay right here till you do.
Oh. You've been lending him some money.
Only a little.
How much?
Only three hundred.
Only three hundred. How much do we spend a month, Jim?
Why--why, about five or six hundred, I guess. Listen, Jack. Bronson'll pay that back. He's in a little trouble. He's made a mistake about a girl out in Woodmere----
And he knows you're famous for being an easy mark, so he comes to you.
No.
You big fool! Did you see that horrible woman you gave your seat to? Why don't you consider me occasionally instead of every fat selfish washwoman you meet?
How should I know----
Jim, did Bronson ever pay you that three hundred?
Why--no, not yet. He was in here last week and he explained that he was a little bit hard up.
I saw it. I heard him say he'd just bought it.
He told me he was hard up.
He was using you! He knew you were easy and he was using you. Can't you see? He wanted you to buy him the car and you did! He's probably roaring his sides out to think how easily he worked you.
Oh, no, you must have mistaken somebody for him----
I'm sorry, Jaqueline. I'll be more careful. I didn't realize what I was doing.
You're the dearest person in the world, but I want all of you and the best of you for me.
Oh, I beg your pardon.
What is it?
Just a minute. Clayton and Drake, Brokers
Morning, Fred.
Morning, Jim. What can I do for you?
Why, a boy's in my office with some stuff C.O.D. and I haven't a cent. Can you let me have fifty till this afternoon?
Sorry, Jim. I've made a rule never to make a personal loan to anybody on any conditions. I've seen it break up too many friendships.
What?
Mr. Edward Lacy.
All right.
Are you busy, Mr. Mather?
Well, not so very.
I'm sorry, Mr. Lacy, but I can't lend you that money.
No?
Girl fainted up here!
Too hot for her!
Just keeled right over!
Get back there! Gangway, you!
Get her out all right?
Say, did you see that?
This damn' company ought to----
Did you see the man that carried her out? He was pale as a ghost, too.
Yes, but did you hear----?
What?

Is this Mr. Lacy? Oh, this is Mather. Why--why, in regard to that matter we talked about this afternoon, I think I'll be able to fix that up after all. James Mather's son, I said-- About that little matter this afternoon----
THE SENSIBLE THING
I want to see you, Mr. Chambers.
Well?
I want to get four days' vacation.
Why, you had a vacation just two weeks ago!
That's true, but now I've got to have another.
Where'd you go last time? To your home?
No, I went to--a place in Tennessee.
Well, where do you want to go this time?
Well, this time I want to go to--a place in Tennessee.
You're consistent, anyhow. But I didn't realize you were employed here as a travelling salesman.
I'm not, but I've got to go.
All right, but you don't have to come back. So don't!
I won't.

I want to thank you. I don't want to come back. I think I'd have gone crazy if you'd said that I could come back. Only I couldn't quit myself, you see, and I want to thank you for--for quitting for me.
Is this street on the way to your house? I don't recognize it.
It's the new boulevard. Jerry just got this car to-day, and he wants to show it to me before he takes us home.
They must like you, that's certain--or they wouldn't let you off twice in three weeks to come down here.
I told them they had to. I told them if they didn't I wouldn't work for them any more.
So glad you're here. Wish you never were going away again, darling.
Do you miss me?
Oh, so much, so much.
Do you--do other men come to see you often? Like those two kids?
Do you expect me never to go anywhere and just fold my hands and sit still--forever?
What do you mean? Do you mean you think I'll never have enough money to marry you?
Oh, don't jump at conclusions so, George.
I'm not jumping at conclusions. That's what you said.
When will you marry me?
Are you ready for me to marry you?
Just when I'm ready to marry you you write me the most nervous letters, as if you're going to back out, and I have to come rushing down here----
You don't have to come if you don't want to.
You'd better go now.
Is something the matter?
I'm going away, Mrs. Cary.
Don't feel so badly, George. If I were you I'd go home to your mother for a week or so. Perhaps after all this is the sensible thing----
I'll come back.
I know you will. And we'll write each other--sometimes.
No, we won't write. I couldn't stand that. Some day I'll come back.
I'll never forget you, George.
Is Miss Jonquil in?
This is she.
Oh--
This is George Rollins. Did you get my letter?
It'll be awfully nice to talk to you again.
I'll be there in about an hour.
This is ridiculous. I don't know exactly what to do. Does my being here bother you?
No.
Are you engaged?
No.
Oh.
Jonquil, after all that's happened between us, I wanted to come back and see you. Whatever I do in the future I'll never love another girl as I've loved you.
You don't love me any more, do you?
No.
I'm going on to Washington in the morning.
I have to go. I've got to be in New York by the first, and meanwhile I want to stop off in Washington.
Business!
A chance for anybody but a fool?
Even for a fool. It was wonderful. Well, I wired New York----
And so, they wired that you ought to take a chance?
Ought to! That I had to. There was no time to lose----
Not a minute?
Not a minute.
Not even time for--
For what?
Gretchen!
Hello, dear. Come see baby.
How long 'fore you'll be down?
Oh, I'll be right down.
Listen, Gretchen beginning with to-night I'm going to--What's the matter?
Nothing. I'm just looking for a cigarette. Go on.
Gretchen-- Well, what is it?
Matches.
Thank you. I didn't mean to interrupt you. Go on.
Gretch----
When you've got time to listen, you might be interested in discussing the poorhouse question with me.
What poorhouse?
Six months ago I left the New York Lithographic Company, and went in the advertising business for myself.
I know, and now instead of getting six hundred a month sure, we're living on a risky five hundred.
Don't worry about me. I'm all right. But you're going to be bored to death sitting here every evening.
No, I won't, except to-night.
What about to-night?
George Tompkins asked us to dinner.
Did you accept?
Of course I did. Why not? You're always talking about what a terrible neighborhood this is, and I thought maybe you'd like to go to a nicer one for a change.
When I go to a nicer neighborhood I want to go for good.
Well, can we go?
We ought to see each other more. You ought to go out more often, old boy. Cocktail?
No, thanks.
No? Well, your fair wife will--won't you, Gretchen?
I love this house.
You look like the devil, Roger. Have a cocktail and cheer up.
Have one.
What? Oh, no, thanks. I've got to work after I get home.
Work! Listen, Roger, you'll kill yourself with work. Why don't you bring a little balance into your life--work a little, then play a little?
That's what I tell him.

Do you know an average business man's day? Coffee in the morning, eight hours' work interrupted by a bolted luncheon, and then home again with dyspepsia and a bad temper to give the wife a pleasant evening.
You've been going to the movies too much.
What? Movies? I've hardly ever been to the movies in my life. I think the movies are atrocious. My opinions on life are drawn from my own observations. I believe in a balanced life.
What's that?
Well probably the best way to tell you would be to describe my own day. Would that seem horribly egotistic?
I can make more money than he can. And I'll be doing it in just forty days.
Forty days. It seems such a long time--when everybody else is always having fun. If I could only sleep for forty days.
Gosh!
I can't help it. They're terrible.
You talk as if I were a child.
I have to.
Gretchen, listen! For God's sake, don't go to pieces now! We're both all stored up with malice and reproach, and if we had a quarrel it'd be terrible. I love you, Gretchen. Say you love me--quick!
You know I love you.
Oh, Roger. I thought you didn't have to work to-night.
I didn't think I'd have to, but something came up.
I've invited George Tompkins over.
Oh, gosh! Well, I'm sorry, honey, but you'll have to phone him not to come.
Oh, hello! We were just discussing you.
Thank you. What particular part of my anatomy was under the scalpel?
Your health.
My health's all right.
Are you implying that my work is useless?
No; not if it brings happiness to some poor sucker of a pants manufacturer who doesn't know how to spend his money.
Oh-h-h! I didn't realize that all these years I've just been wasting my time.
You're a loafer.
What I object to, is that for the last six weeks you seem to have done all your playing around here.
Roger! What do you mean by talking like that?
Just what I said.
You've just lost your temper. You're so nervous from overwork you don't know what you're saying. You're on the verge of a nervous break----
He's acting like a fool, George, but you better get out.
He insulted me! He threatened to throw me out!
He brought it on himself. I've stood as much as my self-respect will allow. I don't want you going out with him any more.
I will go out with him! I'll go out with him all I want! Do you think it's any fun living here with you?
But I don't want to get out.
Well, then, behave yourself. I thought you were going to sleep for this forty days.
Oh, yes, easy enough to say! But I'm tired of sleeping. And what's more, I'm going riding with George Tompkins to-morrow.
You won't go out with him if I have to take you to New York and sit you down in my office until I get through.
Stop! Stop! Stop! Stop! Stop! Stop!
I can't stop. I can't afford to stop.
I don't want any breakfast, except some coffee.
No breakfast?
Going on a trip?
What? Oh, no. That's just some clothes.
Clothes, eh? Well, Mr. Halsey, just to prove that you mean what you say, suppose you let me keep that suitcase until to-morrow noon.
Help yourself.
Just a matter of form.
I understand. Good afternoon.
And don't work too hard, Mr. Halsey. You don't want to have a nervous break----
No. I don't. But I will if you don't leave me alone.
You shouldn't have let him get away with that. What's in there? Clothes?
No. Just all my wife's shoes.
Hello.
Is this the Halsey agency?
Yes, this is Mr. Halsey speaking.
This is Mr. H. G. Garrod.
I called up, young fellow, to say that this is wonderful work you've given us here. We want all of it and as much more as your office can do.
Oh, God!
You have? Can I get a new dress?
Dress? You can get a dozen. This account alone will bring us in forty thousand a year. It's one of the biggest in the West.
Forty thousand a year!
Yes.
Gosh I didn't know it'd really be anything like that. We can have a house like George Tompkins'.
I don't want an interior-decoration shop.
Forty thousand a year! Oh, Roger----
Yes?
I'm not going out with George Tompkins.
I wouldn't let you, even if you wanted to.
Why, I've had a date with him for this Thursday for weeks.
It isn't Thursday.
It is.
It's Friday.
Why, Roger, you must be crazy! Don't you think I know what day it is?
It isn't Thursday. Look!
Yesterday was Wednesday. The laundress came yesterday. I guess I know.
Well, look at the paper. There isn't any question about it.
What's the matter?
I'm scared. I think my nerves are giving away. I can't find any of my shoes.
Your shoes? Why, the closet's full of them.
I know, but I can't see one. Oh, Roger!
Oh, Roger, what's the matter with me? First that newspaper, and now all my shoes. Take care of me, Roger.
I'll get the doctor.
It seems to be in the air this morning.
I got up, and I found that I'd lost a whole day. I had an engagement to go riding with George Tompkins----
What?
George Tompkins won't go riding with any one for many days to come.
Has he gone away?
He's going West.
Why? Is he running away with somebody's wife?
No. He 's had a nervous breakdown.
What?
He just collapsed like an opera-hat in his cold shower.
But he was always talking about his--his balanced life. He had it on his mind.
I know. He's been babbling about it all morning. I think it's driven him a little mad. He worked pretty hard at it, you know.
At what?

At keeping his life balanced. Now all I'll prescribe for this lady here is a good rest. If she'll just stay around the house for a few days and take forty winks of sleep she'll be as fit as ever. She's been under some strain.
Doctor, don't you think I'd better have a rest or something? I've been working pretty hard lately.
You! My boy, I never saw you looking better in your life.
